record.context_brief: Injectivity of the Radon transform under growth conditions
record.original_question: Let Rf denote the classical Radon transform on the plane R^2, defined by integrating a continuous function f over every straight line ℓ_{α,p} = {x ∈ R^2 : α · x = p}, where α is a unit vector and p is real. Assume that f is integrable on every such line, that there exist constants c > 0 and m ≥ 0 with |f(x)| ≤ c(1 + |x|^m) for all x, and that Rf = 0 for every line. Under what weakest natural growth restriction at infinity do these assumptions force f = 0? Equivalently, for which weakest growth conditions is the Radon transform injective on this class of continuous functions?

evidence.quote: Assume that f ∈ L1(ℓα,p ) (2) for all p and α , that f is a continuous function, and that |f (x)| ≤ c(1 + |x|m), (3) where c = const > 0, and m ≥ 0 is a fixed number. Assume that Rf = 0 (4) for all p and α . Problem 1: Does it follow from the above assumptions that f = 0?

The open problem is to understand what the weakest natural restriction on the growth of f at infinity is for the Radon transform to be injective. In other words, under what weakest growth restriction at infinity do assumptions (1) and (3) imply f = 0?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function such that, for every unit vector $\alpha\in S^1$ and every $p\in\mathbb{R}$, the restriction of $f$ to the line $\ell_{\alpha,p}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:\alpha\cdot x=p\}$ is integrable (with respect to one-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the line). Define the Radon transform
$$
(Rf)(\alpha,p)=\int_{\ell_{\alpha,p}} f\,ds,\qquad \alpha\in S^1,\ p\in\mathbb{R}.
$$
Suppose there exist constants $c>0$ and $m\ge 0$ such that
$$
|f(x)|\le c(1+|x|^m)\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^2,
$$
and that $(Rf)(\alpha,p)=0$ for every $\alpha\in S^1$ and every $p\in\mathbb{R}$.

Question: Does it follow that $f\equiv 0$? More generally, determine the weakest natural growth restriction at infinity on a continuous function $f$ (which is integrable along every line) under which $Rf\equiv 0$ implies $f\equiv 0$; equivalently, identify the weakest such growth condition for which the Radon transform is injective on this class.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of identifying the weakest natural growth condition at infinity ensuring injectivity of the planar Radon transform on continuous functions integrable on every line is posed as an open problem by Ramm and remains unresolved in the literature. Classical results give injectivity under decay (e.g., for compactly supported or rapidly decaying functions), and counterexamples exist for functions that decay only like $|x|^{-2}$, but the sharp threshold for polynomial-type growth is not known.

status_evidence.title: Three open problems in analysis
status_evidence.snippet: Problem 1 asks whether assumptions (1)-(4), including the polynomial growth bound |f(x)| ≤ c(1+|x|^m), imply f = 0.
status_evidence.claim: The growth-condition injectivity question for the Radon transform is explicitly posed as an open problem.

status_evidence.title: Some open problems in analysis - A.G. Ramm
status_evidence.snippet: The open problem is to find the weakest natural growth restriction at infinity on f under which Rf=0 implies f=0.
status_evidence.claim: The weakest-growth version of the injectivity question is restated as open in Ramm's open-problems list.
